Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: HVAC Technician
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Vignette:
Three years ago, Kiet Nguyen was elbow-deep in the condenser coil of a hospital’s rooftop HVAC unit when a corroded pressure valve sheared off. The release was instantaneous. A thick, acrid cloud of refrigerant and solvent fumes billowed across the metal grating. He inhaled before he could step back, the chemical burn lodging in his throat and lungs. His vision spotted, his chest seized, and he dropped his wrench, scrambling toward the ladder with trembling hands. A foreman caught his collar and hauled him to the adjacent rooftop before his legs gave out. By the time paramedics arrived, Kiet was coughing violently, convinced the air itself had turned against him. In the weeks that followed, Kiet’s body refused to settle. His shoulders remained knotted, his breath shallow, and his muscles perpetually braced for another rupture. He was certain that danger could bypass any warning, so he stood in the hallway, counting to ten, then walked to each exterior door and window to test the locks. If the deadbolt felt even slightly resistant, he would turn it again, and again, until the mechanism clicked with absolute certainty. When his wife, Mei, brushed his arm in the kitchen and told him the house was fine, that the air was clean, he nodded but could not absorb her words. He had come to believe that being told he was safe was a hollow promise. His body was constantly on alert, scanning for the first sign of another leak, another breach. Over the months, his daily routines shifted. Kiet avoided relaxing because it felt dangerous to let his guard down, fearing that stillness would leave him completely exposed to another leak. What frightened him most was the loss of control that came with closing his eyes. He also began avoiding being alone in a room or building. When the house was quiet, the silence felt like a trap, so he would leave the front door propped open or drive to a crowded diner just to hear other people’s voices. Stressful situations accumulated in his schedule, and he stopped answering work calls that involved overnight service or tight deadlines, avoiding anything that could be stressful. A single tense conversation could make his throat tighten and his hands shake. His occupation as an HVAC technician had become a landscape of avoided spaces. He no longer trusted his own judgment on valve integrity, and when a client pointed out a faint hiss in his shop’s service bay, Kiet froze, his chest caving in, and had to step outside to steady his breathing. He refused to enter mechanical rooms that required heavy locks, and when he did descend into building basements, he insisted on bringing Mei or a coworker. At home, the distance between him and Mei widened. He stopped eating dinner with her, claiming early shifts, though he was often just sitting in the living room with every interior door wide open, counting the seconds between his breaths while waiting for a phone call that never came. The breaking point came when he realized he could no longer climb ladders. Kiet walked into a community mental health clinic with a referral slip from his primary care doctor, his boots scuffed and his grip tight around his work belt. He was most afraid that his body would never stop scanning for danger, that the constant tension would finally crack something irreparable. What he hoped for, quietly and for the first time, was a way to make sense of the alarms ringing in his chest without having to silence them with exhaustion. He wanted to sit in a room and just breathe.
